syllabus_version.title: CBSE Curriculum for the Academic Year 2026-27

concepts.learning_objective: Describe the political and economic features of the Soviet system that came up after the 1917 revolution.
Explain how the east European countries formed the Second World or socialist bloc led by the USSR.
Identify the bureaucratic, authoritarian and national weaknesses of the Soviet system.
Explain why Gorbachev introduced reforms and what perestroika and glasnost meant.
Trace the sequence of events from 1985 to December 1991 that ended the Soviet Union.
Describe how Russia became the successor state of the Soviet Union and how the CIS was formed.

topics.title: Why did the Soviet Union Disintegrate?

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how military spending, satellite states and shortages led to Soviet economic stagnation.
Analyse how an unaccountable party and stifling administration alienated Soviet citizens.
Evaluate the rise of nationalism in the republics as the most immediate cause of the collapse.
Explain why the collapse of the Soviet bloc ended Cold War confrontations and the arms race.
Analyse the change in power relations that made the US the sole superpower.
Describe the aspirations of the new countries that emerged from the Soviet bloc.
Identify the main features of the shock therapy model of transition to capitalism.
Explain the economic and social consequences of shock therapy in Russia and the region.
Evaluate the state of democratic institutions and the economic revival in post-Soviet states.
Identify the secessionist movements and civil wars in the former Soviet republics.
Explain why Central Asia became a zone of competition between outside powers.
Compare the peaceful split of Czechoslovakia with the violent break-up of Yugoslavia.
Describe the economic, political, military and cultural ties between India and the USSR during the Cold War.
Explain the shared multipolar vision of India and Russia and the benefits each gains from the relationship.
Interpret the popularity of Indian films and culture in post-Soviet countries.
Explain how the Marshall Plan, NATO and the Cold War aided European integration after the Second World War.
Sequence the main stages of European integration from the ECSC to the European Union and the euro.

topics.title: Influence and limits of the European Union

concepts.learning_objective: Describe the economic, political-diplomatic and military influence of the European Union.
Analyse how divergent national policies and Euroskepticism limit the EU's ability to act.

topics.title: ASEAN: origins and the ASEAN Way
topics.ncert_sections: Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN)

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the founding members, founding document and objectives of ASEAN.
Explain the 'ASEAN Way' and ASEAN's emphasis on national sovereignty compared with the EU.

topics.title: ASEAN Community, economy and India
topics.ncert_sections: Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN)

concepts.learning_objective: Name the three pillars of the ASEAN Community and the role of the ASEAN Regional Forum.
Explain the objectives of the ASEAN Economic Community and the outward-looking role in Vision 2020.
Describe India's growing ties with ASEAN through the Look East and Act East policies and trade agreements.

topics.title: The rise of the Chinese economy
topics.ncert_sections: The Rise of the Chinese Economy

concepts.learning_objective: Explain the features and shortcomings of China's Soviet-model command economy.
Describe the step-by-step economic reforms in China from the 1970s onwards.
Evaluate the domestic and international consequences of China's economic rise.
Explain why India and China had limited interaction before the twentieth century.
Describe the 1962 border conflict and its long-term implications for India-China relations.
Analyse the strategic and economic dimensions of India-China relations since the late 1980s.

topics.title: Japan and South Korea as centres of power

concepts.learning_objective: Assess Japan's economic strength and constitutional limits as an alternative centre of power.
Describe South Korea's rapid development and the factors behind its high human development.
Identify the countries and natural boundaries that define South Asia as a region.
Describe the mixed democratic record of South Asian countries and the shared aspiration for democracy.

topics.title: The Military and Democracy in Pakistan
topics.ncert_sections: The Military and Democracy in Pakistan

concepts.learning_objective: Trace the sequence of military and elected governments in Pakistan.
Explain the factors that have prevented Pakistan from building a stable democracy.
Explain the causes and course of the struggle that led to the creation of Bangladesh in 1971.
Describe how Bangladesh moved between presidential, military and representative democratic rule after 1971.
Describe the struggle between the monarchy and pro-democracy forces in Nepal up to the 2006 movement.
Explain the role of the Maoists and the challenges in Nepal's transition to a democratic republic.

topics.title: Ethnic Conflict and Democracy in Sri Lanka
topics.ncert_sections: Ethnic Conflict and Democracy in Sri Lanka

concepts.learning_objective: Explain the origins and course of the Sinhala-Tamil ethnic conflict in Sri Lanka.
Describe India's 1987 intervention in Sri Lanka through the Indian Peace Keeping Force and its outcome.
Evaluate Sri Lanka's economic and human development record despite the civil conflict.
Explain the Kashmir issue and the strategic and nuclear dimensions of the India-Pakistan conflict.
Describe the river water and Sir Creek disputes between India and Pakistan and how they have been handled.
Distinguish the areas of disagreement and cooperation between India and Bangladesh.
Describe the special features and the irritants in India-Nepal relations.
Analyse India's relations with Sri Lanka, Bhutan and the Maldives and the mutual perceptions of India and its smaller neighbours.
Explain the aims, achievements and limitations of SAARC and SAFTA.
Identify the measures taken to manage tensions and build peace between India and Pakistan.
Evaluate the role of China and the United States in South Asian politics.
Explain that an international organisation is created by and responds to states and is not a super-state.
Explain why problems such as disease and global warming need international cooperation and how organisations help states cooperate.

topics.title: Evolution of the UN
topics.ncert_sections: Evolution of the UN; Founding of the United Nations

concepts.learning_objective: Describe how the UN emerged as the successor to the League of Nations and state its main objectives.
Recall the key events and dates in the founding of the United Nations.
Identify the principal bodies and specialised agencies of the UN and the issues they handle.

topics.title: Reform of the UN after the Cold War
topics.ncert_sections: Reform of the UN after the Cold War; Reform of Structures and Processes

concepts.learning_objective: Distinguish between reform of the UN's structures and processes and a review of the issues within its jurisdiction.
Identify the changes in world politics after the Cold War that created demands for UN reform.
Evaluate the criteria proposed for new members of the Security Council and the problems with each.

topics.title: The Security Council and the Veto
topics.ncert_sections: Reform of Structures and Processes (membership and veto)

concepts.learning_objective: State the composition of the Security Council and the terms of its permanent and non-permanent members.
Explain what the veto is and how a single permanent member can stall a decision.
Analyse the arguments for abolishing or retaining the veto power.
Recall the steps agreed by world leaders in September 2005 to make the UN more relevant.
Analyse why the decisions on the UN's jurisdiction remain contentious.
Explain India's position on restructuring the UN and expanding the Security Council.
Identify the grounds on which India claims a permanent seat in the Security Council.
Analyse the concerns that make some countries reluctant to accept India as a permanent member.

topics.title: The UN in a Unipolar World
topics.ncert_sections: The UN in a Unipolar World

concepts.learning_objective: Explain why the UN cannot easily check the power of the US.
Evaluate how the UN still serves as a space for dialogue between the US and the rest of the world.

topics.title: Other International Organisations and NGOs
topics.ncert_sections: Boxes: IMF, World Bank, WTO, IAEA, Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch

concepts.learning_objective: Describe the functions of the IMF and the World Bank and the criticisms made of them.
State the purpose and origin of the WTO and the IAEA.
Distinguish human rights NGOs such as Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch from intergovernmental organisations.
Explain security as freedom from threats to core values.
Explain why security relates only to extremely dangerous threats to core values.
Recognise that conceptions of security vary across societies and over time.
Identify the choices a state has when threatened by war, including deterrence and defence.
Explain balance of power and alliance building as components of traditional security policy.
Explain why, without a central world authority, each state is responsible for its own security.
Explain why powerful states focused on external threats after the Second World War.
Describe the external and internal security challenges of newly independent states.
State the accepted limits on the ends and means of war.
Distinguish disarmament from arms control with treaty examples.
Explain confidence building as a means of avoiding violence between rivals.
Compare the referent of security in traditional and non-traditional conceptions.
Distinguish the narrow and broad concepts of human security.
Explain why global threats led to the idea of global security.
Define terrorism and describe debates on human rights as security issues.
Distinguish migrants, refugees and internally displaced people and link them to poverty and conflict.
Explain how epidemics threaten security and the criterion that limits what counts as a security issue.

topics.title: Cooperative Security and India's Security Strategy

concepts.learning_objective: Explain why non-traditional threats need cooperation and collectively sanctioned force.
Describe the four components of India's security strategy with examples.
Explain why environmental degradation is a subject of world politics and not only of geography.
Trace the growing political profile of environmental concerns from the 1960s, including the Club of Rome and UNEP.
Describe the Rio Earth Summit of 1992, its outcomes and the differing agendas of the global North and South.
Define global commons and identify the areas that form part of them.
Describe the environmental importance of Antarctica and the rules governing it.
Analyse why cooperation over the global commons is difficult and shaped by North-South inequality.
Explain the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and the North-South debate behind it.
Describe the UNFCCC and the Kyoto Protocol and why developing countries were exempted from its requirements.
Explain the meaning of common property resources and the reasons for their decline.
Describe sacred groves in India as an example of community-based resource management and its problems.
Explain India's negotiating position based on historical responsibility and per capita emissions.
Identify the programmes and laws through which India participates in global environmental efforts.
Explain India's demand for financial resources and clean technology from developed countries.
Explain why diversity is an important trait of contemporary environmental movements.
Compare the forest and wilderness perspectives of the North and the South.
Describe movements against mining companies and mega-dams with examples.
Explain the meaning of resource geopolitics and how powers have sought secure access to resources.
Analyse the importance of oil and the Gulf region in global strategy.
Explain how shared freshwater resources can become a source of conflict between states.

topics.title: The Indigenous Peoples and Their Rights

concepts.learning_objective: State the UN definition of indigenous populations and their international organisation.
Explain why land is central to the survival and rights of indigenous peoples.
Describe the situation of Scheduled Tribes in India as indigenous people.
Explain globalisation as flows of ideas, capital, commodities and people that create worldwide interconnectedness.
Recognise that globalisation has political, economic and cultural dimensions and an uneven impact.
Explain that the scale and speed of flows distinguish contemporary globalisation from earlier periods.
Describe how technological advances have made the flows of globalisation possible.
Explain why recognition of global interconnections is needed for globalisation.
Explain how globalisation erodes state capacity and replaces the welfare state with a minimalist state.
Evaluate why the state remains important and can even gain capacity through new technology.
Describe economic globalisation as greater flows of commodities, capital and ideas involving many actors.
Explain why the movement of people has not grown as much as other flows.
Compare the arguments of critics and advocates of economic globalisation.
Explain cultural homogenisation and the idea of US soft power and McDonaldisation.
Explain how outside influences can enlarge choices and make cultures more distinctive.
Describe India's colonial economic role and its policy of protectionism after independence.
Evaluate India's 1991 economic reforms against the test of shared benefits of growth.

topics.title: Resistance to Globalisation
topics.ncert_sections: Resistance to Globalisation; India and Resistance to Globalisation

concepts.learning_objective: Distinguish the criticisms of globalisation made by the political left and right.
Describe global platforms of resistance such as the Seattle protests and the World Social Forum.
Identify forms of resistance to globalisation in India from different quarters.
